It predicts that students would benefit from clear instructions, regular feedback, and an opportunity to report unexpected problems. The proposal also acknowledges that participation should remain voluntary during the first semester. Reference case 201001111 makes this reading unique.
questions.listeningTranscript: In the listening response, a student supports testing the proposal but questions one assumption. The student explains that replication studies may help some participants, yet a fixed schedule could exclude students with laboratory work or part-time jobs. Instead of rejecting the plan, the student recommends offering two schedules and comparing the results. This would preserve the committee's goal while producing evidence about access and implementation. Listening case 201001111.

questions.sampleResponse: The reading supports a limited pilot of replication studies, emphasizing clear guidance and regular feedback. The listening does not reject the pilot, but it challenges the assumption that one schedule will serve every student. Because laboratory work and jobs create different time constraints, the speaker recommends two schedules. This adjustment would preserve the proposal's purpose while producing more representative evidence. Sample 201001111.
questions.professorPrompt: Professor Chen asks: When a university tests a new program, should it prioritize quick results or equal access? Explain your view and respond to the ideas below. Discussion 201001111.

studentResponses.response: Quick results matter because a pilot must show whether the idea deserves more funding. A short, focused test can reveal major problems early. Case 201001111.
Equal access matters more because a program tested with only convenient participants may produce a misleading conclusion. Case 201001111.
